question:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the question that follows.

Passage:
In many Indian villages, a woman who needs money for a sewing machine or a few goats has traditionally had only one option: the local moneylender, who may charge interest so high that the loan becomes a trap rather than a help. Self-help groups offer an alternative. A dozen or so women pool small, regular savings, and the common fund is lent to members at modest rates. Because the borrowers are neighbours who know and depend on one another, social pressure, rather than legal threat, ensures that loans are repaid, and defaults are remarkably rare. The benefits extend beyond money. Women who once never left their homes without permission learn to keep accounts, negotiate with bank officials, and speak at public meetings. Their growing confidence often spills into the household, where they begin to take part in decisions about children's education and health. Sceptics warn that such groups cannot replace formal banks, and they are right in a narrow sense: the amounts involved are small. But their real contribution lies elsewhere. They prove that the poor are not unbankable; they are merely underserved.

Question: Why are loan defaults remarkably rare in self-help groups, according to the passage?

options.text: Social pressure among neighbours ensures repayment
Strict legal action is taken against defaulters
The loans are given only to wealthy women
The moneylender guarantees every loan

explanation: पैसेज के अनुसार उधार लेने वाली महिलाएँ पड़ोसी होती हैं जो एक-दूसरे को जानती हैं और एक-दूसरे पर निर्भर हैं; इसलिए कानूनी धमकी नहीं, बल्कि सामाजिक दबाव चुकौती सुनिश्चित करता है।

question:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the question that follows.

Passage:
Every major technological advance has provoked the fear that machines will leave human beings without work. The fear is not groundless: the mechanised loom did destroy the livelihood of hand weavers, and automation continues to displace workers in factories and offices. Yet history also shows that new technologies create employment even as they destroy it. Few people in the early twentieth century could have imagined careers in software, aviation or digital design. The difficulty is that the new jobs seldom appear in the same place, or require the same skills, as the old ones. A displaced factory worker cannot overnight become a data analyst, and the interval between the disappearance of one occupation and the emergence of another can be painful. Artificial intelligence sharpens this concern because it can perform tasks, such as writing and analysis, that were once believed to be the exclusive preserve of educated professionals. The sensible response is neither panic nor complacency, but investment in education and retraining so that workers can move with the change instead of being crushed beneath it.

Question: What does the author say about the fear that machines will leave people without work?

options.text: The fear is entirely baseless
The fear has never been justified by history
New technologies create no new jobs
The fear is not groundless, but new technologies also create employment

explanation: लेखक कहते हैं कि डर निराधार नहीं है (करघे ने बुनकरों की रोज़ी छीनी), पर इतिहास यह भी दिखाता है कि नई तकनीकें रोज़गार पैदा भी करती हैं।

question:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the question that follows.

Passage:
A museum is often imagined as a dusty building where objects are kept behind glass for the benefit of a few scholars. This picture has long been out of date. The best museums today act as bridges between the past and the present, using artefacts to tell stories that help citizens understand who they are and where they come from. A rusted tool, a faded letter, or a fragment of pottery may look unimpressive, but each carries evidence of how ordinary people lived, worked and thought. Museums also protect heritage from the careless destruction that follows economic development, when old buildings are pulled down and traditions forgotten because they seem to have no market value. Critics complain that the exhibits are meant for tourists and not for local people, and in some cases the complaint is justified. The remedy, however, is not to close museums but to open them wider, through free entry days, programmes for schoolchildren, and displays in regional languages. A nation that does not know its past, after all, can hardly be trusted to shape its future wisely.

Question: Which of the following best captures the central idea of the passage?

options.text: Modern museums connect the past with the present and should be made more accessible to all
Museums are dusty buildings meant only for scholars
Museums should be closed because they serve tourists
Old buildings should be pulled down for economic growth

explanation: पैसेज बताता है कि आधुनिक संग्रहालय अतीत और वर्तमान के बीच पुल हैं, और आलोचना का समाधान उन्हें बंद करना नहीं बल्कि अधिक सुलभ बनाना है।

question:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the question that follows.

Passage:
For decades, air pollution was treated as an inconvenience of industrial life, a smudge on the horizon that bothered the eyes but threatened little else. Medical research has since overturned this comfortable belief. Fine particles, small enough to pass through the nose and lungs into the bloodstream, are now linked to heart disease, strokes, and reduced lung growth in children. The damage is often silent and cumulative; a person may appear healthy for years before the effects show themselves. What makes the problem especially difficult to tackle is that no single culprit can be blamed. Vehicles, power plants, construction dust, and the burning of crop residue each add their share, and measures that curb one source may leave the others untouched. Cities that have succeeded in clearing their skies, such as those that restricted traffic and shifted to cleaner fuels, did so through sustained and coordinated effort, not through emergency measures taken once the smog had already descended. Clean air is, in the end, less a matter of technology than of political will.

Question: How was air pollution viewed for decades, according to the passage?

options.text: As an inconvenience that bothered the eyes but threatened little else
As the main cause of heart disease
As a problem that affected only children
As a danger that could be removed overnight

explanation: पैसेज की पहली पंक्ति के अनुसार दशकों तक प्रदूषण को औद्योगिक जीवन की एक असुविधा माना गया जो आँखों को खटकती थी, पर और कोई खास खतरा नहीं थी।

Passage:
For decades, air pollution was treated as an inconvenience of industrial life, a smudge on the horizon that bothered the eyes but threatened little else. Medical research has since overturned this comfortable belief. Fine particles, small enough to pass through the nose and lungs into the bloodstream, are now linked to heart disease, strokes, and reduced lung growth in children. The damage is often silent and cumulative; a person may appear healthy for years before the effects show themselves. What makes the problem especially difficult to tackle is that no single culprit can be blamed. Vehicles, power plants, construction dust, and the burning of crop residue each add their share, and measures that curb one source may leave the others untouched. Cities that have succeeded in clearing their skies, such as those that restricted traffic and shifted to cleaner fuels, did so through sustained and coordinated effort, not through emergency measures taken once the smog had already descended. Clean air is, in the end, less a matter of technology than of political will.

question:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the question that follows.

Passage:
It is often said that sport builds character, and the claim is repeated so frequently that it is rarely examined. Does a game really make a person honest, disciplined and generous? Not automatically. A child who is taught only to win at any cost may learn to cheat, to sneer at opponents, and to blame others for failure. Sport shapes character only when it is accompanied by the right values: respect for rules, grace in defeat, and humility in victory. Coaches therefore bear a heavy responsibility, since young players imitate what they see more readily than what they are told. When a coach praises effort over outcome and treats a defeated rival with courtesy, the lesson is absorbed without a single lecture. The same is true of spectators. A crowd that jeers at a missed catch teaches its children that failure deserves contempt, whereas one that applauds a gallant loser teaches them the opposite. The playing field can be a school of life, but only if someone is willing to teach there.

Question: What does the author say about the claim that sport builds character?

options.text: It holds true only when sport is accompanied by the right values
It is true automatically for every player
It is completely false
It applies only to professional players

explanation: लेखक कहते हैं 'Not automatically'; खेल चरित्र तभी बनाता है जब उसके साथ नियमों का सम्मान, हार में गरिमा और जीत में विनम्रता जैसे सही मूल्य जुड़े हों।
